name: Fully Furnished Cozy Apartment
description: This cozy space is a wonder of post-Katrina recovery detailing.  Finely finished doors, cabinets, and wood molding are made from Katrina debris.  The hand-painted floors are a marvel of trompe-l'œil ingenuity.
neighborhood_overview: NorthWest Carrollton, where this apartment is located, is a New Orleans neighborhood bounded by Leonidas Street, Earhart Blvd., Carrollton Avenue and Claiborne Avenue.  We're the “northern” (aka lakeside) peninsula of Carrollton, a historic neighborhood on the National Historic Register.  Craftsman bungalows and raised-basement houses join a mix of early 20th-century house types and styles to define Northwest Carrollton's visual personality. Businesses along Earhart and South Claiborne serve the neighborhood's commercial needs, while Ye Olde College Inn and Rock 'n' Bowl on Carrollton number among the many dining and recreational opportunities. If you aren't sure where Northwest Carrollton is located, just look for the lion statues atop pedestals that herald the entrance to Pritchard Place, developed in 1913.

I speak Spanish fluently.  International guests always welcome.

Part of the charm of this house is its location near the center of New Orleans culture. Located 2 blocks from the French Quarter on one of the wider residential streets in old New Orleans, this house offers the convenience of access to New Orleans night life when you want it and the quiet seclusion of a neighborhood when you don’t. description:
Our turn-of-the-century Caribbean-style home offers a peaceful retreat in the best neighborhood in NOLA. We are fully licensed and an easy 15 min stroll to the French Quarter with plenty to enjoy along the way.

All awesome and well-behaved pets are welcome!

We use professional cleaners to keep things fresh and safe between guests while keeping things cozy.

neighborhood_overview:
Maison du Madison is nestled in Marigny an area that runs into the French Quarter and is known for its artsy vibe, music scene, hip coffee shops, outstanding restaurants, murals, and colorful turn of the century cottages.

Take a stroll, grab a coffee, and you'll be downtown before you realize it without having to deal with the noise (and bachelor parties) of downtown. Or stay put and take a swing lesson at Allways Lounge, explore live music on Frenchmen, show off your own pipes at Kajuns Karaoke, up your social media photo game at JAM, and eat at some of the best cafes and restaurants in town.

We're also 2 blocks from the hippest hood in Nola, Bywater. Bywater's vibe has been described as "what Brooklyn is trying to be." It's full of musicians and artists, murals, gardens, and more coffee shops, and restaurants. It's got fabulous rummage shops where you'll enjoy digging for antique finds, outstanding people watching, alfresco jazz spots with wine and cheese,
host_about:

I enjoy seeing the world and helping others see my town as I do; magical, irreverent, and like no place else on earth. Thank you for checking out my profile. Come down to Nola and stay with us, you'll be glad you did.

neighborhood_overview:
Faubourg Marigny was actually the 1st subdivision in New Orleans that developed from a factory area to the culturally rich neighborhood filled with Creole cottages that it is today.

The City of New Orleans started with just the area now known as the “Vieux Carre,” or the “French Quarter.” New Orleans grew north from Rampart Street into what is now Faubourg Treme, eventually linking up to Bayou St. John, in what is now “Mid City.” As the city continued to grow, plantation owners began breaking up their tracts of land into smaller lots to sell to newcomers. The first plantation owner to do this, Bernard Marigny de Mandeville, owned the land just downriver from Esplanade Avenue.

As more and more French people came to the area, the demand for residential property became greater. By 1805, exiles from both France and Haiti flocked to the city in the wake of revolutions. Forty years of Spanish control of Louisiana attracted a number of people from Spain and her colonies

neighborhood_overview:
Just down river (east) from the French Quarter - stretching from Press Street to the Industrial Canal - is the Bywater, where the mood and pace shift as you enter into the heart of an edgier yet still welcoming neighborhood. The St. Claude Arts District, centered around St. Claude Avenue, is home to more than thirty locations exhibiting visual and performance art, along with an array of artisan crafts. Down Piety Street, the fun continues with restaurants, thrift stores and more galleries. Even the homes, cafes and restaurants seem to capture Bywater's eclectic appreciation for the arts.

Afterward, you can thrift your way through the neighborhood before stopping in at an exhibition and finally making your way to dinner. The area's restaurants are among the most innovative in the city and are great places to sit with a cocktail and chat with locals.

host_about:
I grew up about 90 miles from New Orleans and after living in several cities around the U.S. I settled here in 2000 and continue to fall in love with the city ... My favorite area is called Frenchman Street because there is the heart of the live music scene with approximately 12 music clubs within a 3 block stretch  offering live music 7 nights a week ... Since 2010 I hosted over 250 guests at my home in the French Quarter, first, and then my home in the Marigny Neighborhood via the website couch surfing dot org ... So I'm new to airbnb but shouldn't be for long with Voodoo Festival coming up and then Mardi Gras, and not long after that Jazz Fest ... Happy travels to you and I hope to see you in New Orleans ...

Six things I like to do: Philosophy Cafe in New Orleans, Swing dance camp in July in Sweden, Garden Festival in Croatia, Live music on Frenchman Street,  Work - I love to make my properties nice places to live, and Meditation - my quiet still time with myself.

As hosts, either myself or my business partner Joann, will attempt to make your stay in NoLa as close to perfect as we can.

As a guest I will barely be seen as I will probably have much to do with not much time to do it ... and clean, orderly, and respectful.

When I travel I have been preferring hostels and friends but now I will be discovering airbnb as well.

Motto - Enjoy! and if you can, do some good.

host_about:
“The first thing you notice about New Orleans are the burying grounds - the cemeteries - and they're a cold proposition, one of the best things there are here. Going by, you try to be as quiet as possible, better to let them sleep. Greek, Roman, sepulchres- palatial mausoleums made to order, phantomesque, signs and symbols of hidden decay - ghosts of women and men who have sinned and who've died and are now living in tombs. The past doesn't pass away so quickly here. You could be dead for a long time.

The ghosts race towards the light, you can almost hear the heavy breathing spirits, all determined to get somewhere. New Orleans, unlike a lot of those places you go back to and that don't have the magic anymore, still has got it. Night can swallow you up, yet none of it touches you. Around any corner, there's a promise of something daring and ideal and things are just getting going. There's something obscenely joyful behind every door, either that or somebody crying with their head in their hands. A lazy rhythm looms in the dreamy air and the atmosphere pulsates with bygone duels, past-life romance, comrades requesting comrades to aid them in some way. You can't see it, but you know it's here. Somebody is always sinking. Everyone seems to be from some very old Southern families. Either that or a foreigner. I like the way it is.

There are a lot of places I like, but I like New Orleans better. There's a thousand different angles at any moment. At any time you could run into a ritual honoring some vaguely known queen. Bluebloods, titled persons like crazy drunks, lean weakly against the walls and drag themselves through the gutter. Even they seem to have insights you might want to listen to. No action seems inappropriate here. The city is one very long poem. Gardens full of pansies, pink petunias, opiates. Flower-bedecked shrines, white myrtles, bougainvillea and purple oleander stimulate your senses, make you feel cool and clear inside.

Everything in New Orleans is a good idea. Bijou temple-type cottages and lyric cathedrals side by side. Houses and mansions, structures of wild grace. Italianate, Gothic, Romanesque, Greek Revival standing in a long line in the rain. Roman Catholic art. Sweeping front porches, turrets, cast-iron balconies, colonnades- 30-foot columns, gloriously beautiful- double pitched roofs, all the architecture of the whole wide world and it doesn't move. All that and a town square where public executions took place. In New Orleans you could almost see other dimensions. There's only one day at a time here, then it's tonight and then tomorrow will be today again. Chronic melancholia hanging from the trees. You never get tired of it. After a while you start to feel like a ghost from one of the tombs, like you're in a wax museum below crimson clouds. Spirit empire. Wealthy empire. One of Napoleon's generals, Lallemaud, was said to have come here to check it out, looking for a place for his commander to seek refuge after Waterloo. He scouted around and left, said that here the devil is damned, just like everybody else, only worse. The devil comes here and sighs. New Orleans. Exquisite, old-fashioned. A great place to live vicariously. Nothing makes any difference and you never feel hurt, a great place to really hit on things. Somebody puts something in front of you here and you might as well drink it. Great place to be intimate or do nothing. A place to come and hope you'll get smart - to feed pigeons looking for handouts” bob dylan

host_about:
Folwell Dunbar: An Abridged (and slightly fictitious) Autobiography 

Fol·well \ fόl-wel \ n, pl. Folwells [from the Cajun Faux and Weeeeeee] This highly endangered and elusive species (folwellius dunbarian, estimated population: 1. Common names include Foz, Fu, Fuzzy, Foly and Fu-Bear) was first discovered in the mid 1960s along the creosote shores of Bayou Bonfuca. Genetic research has shown that it was first conceived in Mexico, carried north by a band of Olmec nomads and finally deposited beneath a bald cypress tree in the Honey Island Swamp. Legend has it that an osprey had landed there with a cottonmouth in its talons. The young child was then placed in a pirogue and set adrift. He was soon discovered by a den of aquatic reptilian royalty and nursed to maturity by a particularly handsome, nine-foot she-gator. Once weaned, the young Folwell began feeding on “nutra rats,” water hyacinth and other vile, invasive species. Eventually, the young hominid left its adopted home and sojourned northward to the glaciated reaches of Massachusetts for some good, wholesome Puritanical book learnin. After four frostbitten years of preppy, intellectual enlightenment, Folwell carpetbagged it back south to the gothic tobacco barns of Durham, North Carolina. After another “cough, cough,” four years of higher order thinking and lower order wrestling at Duke University, he ventured to the hinterlands of South America. In Zhumar, Ecuador (pop. 54 on a good day!), he culled rogue sheep, raised rainbow trout in earthen ponds, cooked guinea pigs over an open fire, kept “killer” bees, and drank lots of spittle-tainted chicha and kerosene-toxic trago. Once again though, after almost three years of Andean bliss and Atawalpa’s revenge, the wander-lustful neotropical migrant set off. He trekked along the Ruta Maya, past the land of United Fruit and through the fields of the Zapatistas, until he finally settled in the true “Banana Republic” of Louisiana. In the Big Queasy, he taught Ancient, US and World History, Spanish and First Grade. He studied at Tulane and juggled on Decatur Street, until, once again, he took flight. Landing in the virtual reality of the Research Triangle Park, he helped found a school for techno-savvy cyber children, coached wrestling, and visited countless, generic shopping malls. After only two years in CARY (Concentrated Area of Relocated Yankees), he was drawn back to the Big Queasy by the ethereal beat of Satchmo, Sidney Bichet, and of course Professor Longhair. There, he set out on a quest for comprehensive whole-school reform, a.k.a. Peace Corps with a paycheck. He scooped and delivered dollops of PD, scribbled reams of educational, jargon-infused drivel, and beat the drum loudly for improved teaching and learning.   Folwell, his wife Lucia, and their shaggy and occasionally obedient black dog live in an ancient and decrepit shotgun doublewide, two blocks from Desire (of Streetcar fame), a levee away from Old Man River, and a hop, a skip and a short stagger from the Vieux Carre’. They can be found fighting the stupids, social working, and generally barking around…

host_about:
“The first thing you notice about New Orleans are the burying grounds - the cemeteries - and they're a cold proposition, one of the best things there are here. Going by, you try to be as quiet as possible, better to let them sleep. Greek, Roman, sepulchres- palatial mausoleums made to order, phantomesque, signs and symbols of hidden decay - ghosts of women and men who have sinned and who've died and are now living in tombs. The past doesn't pass away so quickly here. You could be dead for a long time.

The ghosts race towards the light, you can almost hear the heavy breathing spirits, all determined to get somewhere. New Orleans, unlike a lot of those places you go back to and that don't have the magic anymore, still has got it. Night can swallow you up, yet none of it touches you. Around any corner, there's a promise of something daring and ideal and things are just getting going. There's something obscenely joyful behind every door, either that or somebody crying with their head in their hands. A lazy rhythm looms in the dreamy air and the atmosphere pulsates with bygone duels, past-life romance, comrades requesting comrades to aid them in some way. You can't see it, but you know it's here. Somebody is always sinking. Everyone seems to be from some very old Southern families. Either that or a foreigner. I like the way it is.

There are a lot of places I like, but I like New Orleans better. There's a thousand different angles at any moment. At any time you could run into a ritual honoring some vaguely known queen. Bluebloods, titled persons like crazy drunks, lean weakly against the walls and drag themselves through the gutter. Even they seem to have insights you might want to listen to. No action seems inappropriate here. The city is one very long poem. Gardens full of pansies, pink petunias, opiates. Flower-bedecked shrines, white myrtles, bougainvillea and purple oleander stimulate your senses, make you feel cool and clear inside.

Everything in New Orleans is a good idea. Bijou temple-type cottages and lyric cathedrals side by side. Houses and mansions, structures of wild grace. Italianate, Gothic, Romanesque, Greek Revival standing in a long line in the rain. Roman Catholic art. Sweeping front porches, turrets, cast-iron balconies, colonnades- 30-foot columns, gloriously beautiful- double pitched roofs, all the architecture of the whole wide world and it doesn't move. All that and a town square where public executions took place. In New Orleans you could almost see other dimensions. There's only one day at a time here, then it's tonight and then tomorrow will be today again. Chronic melancholia hanging from the trees. You never get tired of it. After a while you start to feel like a ghost from one of the tombs, like you're in a wax museum below crimson clouds. Spirit empire. Wealthy empire. One of Napoleon's generals, Lallemaud, was said to have come here to check it out, looking for a place for his commander to seek refuge after Waterloo. He scouted around and left, said that here the devil is damned, just like everybody else, only worse. The devil comes here and sighs. New Orleans. Exquisite, old-fashioned. A great place to live vicariously. Nothing makes any difference and you never feel hurt, a great place to really hit on things. Somebody puts something in front of you here and you might as well drink it. Great place to be intimate or do nothing. A place to come and hope you'll get smart - to feed pigeons looking for handouts” bob dylan

name: The Columns Apartment - Historic Algiers Point!
description: Experience New Orleans from a Century Old Home built in 1910! Our Shotgun apartment offers two bedrooms, each with a private entrance. Algiers Point is a quaint village of historic homes and locally owned businesses. A short walk to the Algiers-Canal St. Ferry Terminal,  then a 5 min ride to the French Quarter and Downtown Area. neighborhood_overview:
Algiers Point offers a rich mix of history, architecture and small town charm only minutes away from the world famous French Quarter. Enjoy a short walk to the peaceful ferry, past historic creole cottages, shotgun doubles and majestic Victorians and take in the best view of the city from the Mississippi river levee.

The Point is home to locally owned and operated restaurants, cafes, bars, pubs and a blown glass studio, all located in buildings dating back to 1800's. Algiers Point takes its name from nautical maps that identify the bend in the river as it curves around the neighborhood. The Point was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978 and designated a local historic district in 1994.

A few or our neighborhood favorites (all less than a 10 minute walk):

-Faubourg Fresh Market (small grocery store with all the necessities & some local specialties)

neighborhood_overview: Treme is the musical birthplace of Jazz, Blues, and Soul. It's an area full of soul food, jazz halls, second line parades, and on a main route making it a breeze to walk or grab an über to anywhere in the city. This neighborhood has seen ups and downs in recent history and has quickly been on the rise as one one of the most up and coming neighborhoods in the city. It's been a balancing act to retain its incredible culture with improving its infrastructure and worn exterior. Most of the neighbors here are musicians or children of musicians and all have incredible stories to share if you have the time to listen. This is a social neighborhood that loves to greet each other, this is a major facets of old New Orleans culture still active today.  This is one of the last bits of the real New Orleans left and fun to experience life in the neighborhood that gave us the nickname the Big Easy.
host_about: I look at much of life through a lens. Which works well as I am a commercial photographer in New Orleans and a project manager for a creative resource company in town. Today, with seven blocks and nearly every type of small business imaginable, Oak Street is once again the commercial center and pride of the city's Carrollton neighborhood. Occupying the historic buildings from the 20th century are a collection of coffee shops, art galleries, new and second-hand clothing boutiques, hobby shops, cozy dining establishments and other small businesses.

neighborhood_overview: The 7th Ward is a historic Creole New Orleans' neighborhood. Many of the rich traditions of New Orleans' culture were born in the 7th Ward. host_about:
Aminata: I’ve spent most of my adult life traveling internationally after catching the travel bug as a high school exchange student in France. Africa became my calling during undergrad and after living in Senegal for nearly a year, I went on to complete a year of studies in Ghana and later made Ghana home for five years. During that time I started an African women’s social enterprise and eventually a non-profit to support girls’ education which I still run today. Living abroad for so long and always at the grace of so many kind generous people shaped my outlook on life and what’s really important. After being spoiled by such a different way of being, I was not certain that I could live in the United States long-term but my longing to be near family again made me give it a try. When I came to New Orleans for the first time in 2007, I knew that this was the city for me. So much of what I loved about the people and lifestyle of West Africa is exactly what makes New Orleans the special place that it is.  I moved to New Orleans in 2008 and I have been deeply in love with the city ever since. I know that it is no accident that I now have a beautiful home to host others in a city that calls people from all over the world. I welcome the opportunity to pay forward all of the goodness and hospitality that has been such a fortune for me. I truly believe that this is what makes the world go round and there is no greater joy than sharing the city that makes me so happy with others. 

After a decade living in the city, I was fortunate enough to marry the man of my dreams, Ben E. Hunter, who just happens to be one of New Orleans' most beloved local music celebrities.  

Ben:  I was born and raised in New Orleans, growing up from the Treme to the 7th Ward. I've performed nationally and locally for the past 20+ years as a music artist with seven studio albums recorded in New Orleans, Jamaica, and Los Angeles. Having grown up in this historic neighborhood, it's fascinating to witness the transformation of a place that has such deep roots in the entire fabric of New Orleans' music history. It is a pleasure to introduce a wide range of people from all over the country and the world to our great city and this beautifully unique neighborhood. Our home is truly filled with love and joy and a lust for life that we look forward to sharing with you!

neighborhood_overview:
Our rental is located in the Carrollton area. Carrollton is a historic neighborhood of Uptown New Orleans, Louisiana, which includes the Carrollton Historic District, recognized by the HISTORIC DISTRICT LANDMARK COMMISSION. It is the part of Uptown New Orleans farthest upriver while still being easily accessible to the French Quarter. It was historically a separate town, laid out in 1833 and incorporated on March 10, 1845. Carrollton was annexed by New Orleans in 1874 (becoming the city's 16th and 17th Wards), but it has long retained some elements of distinct identity.

The main street is Carrollton Avenue, lined with Southern live oaks, with the St. Charles Avenue Streetcar running on the "neutral ground" or central median. The streetcar barn is a block off of Carrollton Avenue, on Willow Street, and the landmark Camellia Grill diner is near the corner of St. Charles and Carrollton Avenues.

name: The Townhouse on Magazine  (Lower Garden District)
description: The Townhouse.  Once, a Jazz Age Speakeasy hidden in an 1850's home on Magazine Street. Built in the Lower Garden District in the time of Mark Twain and riverboats, later pouring Gin while Louis Armstrong was king. Today, a luxury New Orleans pied-à-terre. Original architectural decadence paired with modern style, high ceiling and grand scale. Private walled courtyard. Walk to famous Restaurants, Bars, Shopping, Streetcar, Convention Center, WWII Museum. Closest historic neighborhood to Quarter.
neighborhood_overview: The Lower Garden District is one of the best known and loved historic neighborhoods in the city. It is considered the best in terms of it amazing central location being close to everything. It has a reputation of having cool artistic people and its own antebellum park and fountains! Full of shopping and restaurants and right beside the Warehouse district, 3 blocks frome the National WWII Museum and a stones throw from the Convention Center.
host_about:
I was born in New Orleans and raised in the French Quarter. My father moved from his native London as a professional Jazz musician and started his family at this epicenter of fantastic architecture,  amazing food and renowned music. A childhood like that tends to make a permanent impression so after studying architecture and design in college I worked around the country but was drawn back to this wonderful sticky hot magical city. Moving back I realized just how many amazing historic homes in this city were being forgotten and lost. I started on just one project, one house, but it turned out to just be the "first house". I fell in love with a guy who had the same shared passion for design and preservation and now with our daughter in tow, our family  works relentlesly on acquiring and restoring historic architecture. So far we've restored more than a dozen virtually lost houses (mostly in the LGD) and have no plans to stop anytime soon. Almost all of the houses we have brought back were abandoned, partially collapsed "basket cases" (some even had huge trees growing through their roofs). Often it seems the worse they are, the more we want them.  Their former beauty shines through and their history speaks to us.
 You see, we think that the history and romanticism of New Orleans is best conveyed through the preservation and use of its unique architecture, cooking it's amazing food,  and playing it's fantastic music. And well, since we can't boil water or play a single instrument between us, we've decided to concentrate on the houses. We hope you like what we've done; it wasn't easy. You never know, maybe our daughter will grow up to be a chef who plays the clarinet.

name: 2 Floor 1855 Townhouse Suite Lower Garden District
description: The Townhouse Suite. Once part of a speakeasy, hidden in an 1850's home on Magazine Street, now a luxury New Orleans pied-à-terre. Original architectural decadence paired with modern style, high ceilings and grand scale on two floors with a master bedroom loft and an original wrought iron gallery. Walk to famous Restaurants, Boutiques, Bars and Streetcar. French Quarter, Convention Center, WWII Museum just down the street.
host_about:
I was born in New Orleans and raised in the French Quarter. My father moved from his native London as a professional Jazz musician and started his family at this epicenter of fantastic architecture,  amazing food and renowned music. A childhood like that tends to make a permanent impression so after studying architecture and design in college I worked around the country but was drawn back to this wonderful sticky hot magical city. Moving back I realized just how many amazing historic homes in this city were being forgotten and lost. I started on just one project, one house, but it turned out to just be the "first house". I fell in love with a guy who had the same shared passion for design and preservation and now with our daughter in tow, our family  works relentlesly on acquiring and restoring historic architecture. So far we've restored more than a dozen virtually lost houses (mostly in the LGD) and have no plans to stop anytime soon. Almost all of the houses we have brought back were abandoned, partially collapsed "basket cases" (some even had huge trees growing through their roofs). Often it seems the worse they are, the more we want them.  Their former beauty shines through and their history speaks to us.
 You see, we think that the history and romanticism of New Orleans is best conveyed through the preservation and use of its unique architecture, cooking it's amazing food,  and playing it's fantastic music. And well, since we can't boil water or play a single instrument between us, we've decided to concentrate on the houses. We hope you like what we've done; it wasn't easy. You never know, maybe our daughter will grow up to be a chef who plays the clarinet.

neighborhood_overview: The Lower Garden District is often confused with its more famous neighbor, the Upper Garden District, but it has a unique, eclectic flavor all its own. Centered around Coliseum Square, the area is one of graceful vistas and curving streets, replete with classical names like Dryades, Melpomene, and Terpsichore. Indeed, Lee Circle, originally named Tivoli Circle, was envisioned as an anchor for the nine streets that extend from it, all named after the nine muses. The houses here actually predate those of the Garden District proper, since they were built in the early years of the 19th century during the city's upriver expansion from the French Quarter.

neighborhood_overview:
The Bywater is a cool neighborhood of shotgun houses and creole cottages, and is home to a thriving bohemian art scene. It is a bit east (down river) from the French Quarter with a fun mix of local folks who grew up here, and more recent bohemian arrivals. Artists and musicians relocated here when the French Quarter became too pricy. It's not uncommon to hear the sounds of a piano or guitar playing in the afternoon through an open window.

description: Welcome to Uptown New Orleans, where dreams lend themselves to reality in this picturesque pocket of the city. Centrally located to an abundance of day and night life, you and your guests will waste no time wondering what to do first!

THE NEIGHBORHOOD
This is a great residential neighborhood in Uptown New Orleans.

0.5 miles from Tulane and Loyola universities

My goal is to help my Guest make the most of their stay here in The Big Easy.  I want to give a combination of things to see and do that takes you from the Art scene to the Zydeco music  scene. name: Immerse in the Happiness Haven @ the Heart of NOLA
description: Be among the fortunate to stay in this charmed Nola abode! Well situated just one mile from the French Quarter, Jazz Fest, Frenchmen St, and beautiful City Park! This is the heart of New Orleans' best attractions, while anchored in a historic Creole neighborhood that exudes real southern warmth amidst a colorful sampling of New Orleans' architecture. Enjoy old Nawlins' charm with the comfort of the most modern amenities. Great for couples, groups, biz travelers & families.
neighborhood_overview: The 7th Ward is a historic Creole New Orleans' neighborhood. Many of the rich traditions of New Orleans' culture were born in the 7th Ward. Our home was owned by one of the most prominent Creole families in the city making it part of a long history of family and community of which we feel honored to take part. This area of the 7th Ward is known as Esplanade Ridge because of its proximity to Esplanade Ave and its ridge elevation. It is truly an urban neighborhood - a stone's throw to all the happenings but still with a quiet though friendly local community feel. New Orleans continues to change quickly right before our eyes so our neighborhood is quite mixed with families who have been here for generations and many newcomers to the city. This is also a popular neighborhood for AirBnB so you will often see other visitors heading your way.
host_about:
Aminata: I’ve spent most of my adult life traveling internationally after catching the travel bug as a high school exchange student in France. Africa became my calling during undergrad and after living in Senegal for nearly a year, I went on to complete a year of studies in Ghana and later made Ghana home for five years. During that time I started an African women’s social enterprise and eventually a non-profit to support girls’ education which I still run today. Living abroad for so long and always at the grace of so many kind generous people shaped my outlook on life and what’s really important. After being spoiled by such a different way of being, I was not certain that I could live in the United States long-term but my longing to be near family again made me give it a try. When I came to New Orleans for the first time in 2007, I knew that this was the city for me. So much of what I loved about the people and lifestyle of West Africa is exactly what makes New Orleans the special place that it is.  I moved to New Orleans in 2008 and I have been deeply in love with the city ever since. I know that it is no accident that I now have a beautiful home to host others in a city that calls people from all over the world. I welcome the opportunity to pay forward all of the goodness and hospitality that has been such a fortune for me. I truly believe that this is what makes the world go round and there is no greater joy than sharing the city that makes me so happy with others. 

After a decade living in the city, I was fortunate enough to marry the man of my dreams, Ben E. Hunter, who just happens to be one of New Orleans' most beloved local music celebrities.  

Ben:  I was born and raised in New Orleans, growing up from the Treme to the 7th Ward. I've performed nationally and locally for the past 20+ years as a music artist with seven studio albums recorded in New Orleans, Jamaica, and Los Angeles. Having grown up in this historic neighborhood, it's fascinating to witness the transformation of a place that has such deep roots in the entire fabric of New Orleans' music history. It is a pleasure to introduce a wide range of people from all over the country and the world to our great city and this beautifully unique neighborhood. Our home is truly filled with love and joy and a lust for life that we look forward to sharing with you!

host_about:
I was born in New Orleans and raised in the French Quarter. My father moved from his native London as a professional Jazz musician and started his family at this epicenter of fantastic architecture,  amazing food and renowned music. A childhood like that tends to make a permanent impression so after studying architecture and design in college I worked around the country but was drawn back to this wonderful sticky hot magical city. Moving back I realized just how many amazing historic homes in this city were being forgotten and lost. I started on just one project, one house, but it turned out to just be the "first house". I fell in love with a guy who had the same shared passion for design and preservation and now with our daughter in tow, our family  works relentlesly on acquiring and restoring historic architecture. So far we've restored more than a dozen virtually lost houses (mostly in the LGD) and have no plans to stop anytime soon. Almost all of the houses we have brought back were abandoned, partially collapsed "basket cases" (some even had huge trees growing through their roofs). Often it seems the worse they are, the more we want them.  Their former beauty shines through and their history speaks to us.
 You see, we think that the history and romanticism of New Orleans is best conveyed through the preservation and use of its unique architecture, cooking it's amazing food,  and playing it's fantastic music. And well, since we can't boil water or play a single instrument between us, we've decided to concentrate on the houses. We hope you like what we've done; it wasn't easy. You never know, maybe our daughter will grow up to be a chef who plays the clarinet.

host_about:
I am a small business owner in the mid city area New Orleans. I absolutely love this city the food the music the festivals and I do it all. 

Myself I’m a big FOODIE.  I have my favorites from neighborhood joints down the street to the White tablecloth Michelin star/James Beard award winning restaurants. Great thing about New Orleans you can find really YUM food just about anywhere. Many neighborhood joints have James Beard award winning chefs.  I am always discovering a new fave. 

Music I love live entertainment and we have GREAT Music venues throughout the city from the outdoor concerts, to the local dives or the seated performances at The Auditorium in Armstrong Park. 

Who doesn’t love a great Bar scene. New Orleans has many Bars in many neighborhoods. Starting with Bourbon St in The French Quarters, how about a hole in the wall in the Historic Treme’ or a  pool bar in the Bywater, Frenchmen St in the Marigny neighborhood and Magazine St in the Irish Channel. The list goes on and on and on. Lol 
 
We also have many great museums throughout the city everything’s on exhibit from our Culture to the history of the City. We have one of the best children’s museums completely hands on this is always a wonderful afternoon with the kids. New Orleans Museum of Art in City Park is one of my favorite because after touring the museum it’s a short walk through the park for Cafe’ o latte and Beignets at Café Du Monde’ City park location With indoor and outdoor dining. City Park is filled with many live oak trees. 

My goal is to help my Guest make the most of their stay here in The Big Easy.  I want to give a combination of things to see and do that takes you from the Art scene to the Zydeco music  scene.  I want to help you discover more than just the French Quarters I want you to have a real sense of what this city and our people are about by the time you leave. :-) 

Laissez les bons temps rouler
“Let the good times roll”

host_about:
I'm Cody (left) and with my husband, Leo (right) in our June 2019 vacation photo from Mexico.  When we're not on our own vacations, we love to make yours the best it can be! We’re excited to own our first renovation home together in New Orleans. I’m a math teacher and he’s a research and development scientist. We love our home in the 7th Ward! 

Leo has been in New Orleans since 2008 and had an incredible home in the Marigny on Burgundy.  As chance would have it, we met at a house party in the French Quarter in 2016. Having lived all my adult life in St. Louis, I was in New Orleans for the 3rd time with friends and a party with locals sounded great.  We crossed paths when we were both talking to the same cute rugby boy from Atlanta and decided we were more interested in each other! The next 3 days we broke the rules of Southern Decadence and spent all the time together! We decided that long-distance was worth a shot when you hit it off this well.  We ended up never going more than 10 days without seeing each other in person for the next four months.  Teachers are in short supply in New Orleans, so by Christmas we were engaged and I had moved here.  We got married exactly one year after we met, in the exact same spot where we met with our closest friends around us.  Three weeks later, we closed on this house and began our home renovation.  It's been a LOT of work and a long haul, but we love the way our home is coming together! 

We opened up the rental suite to our first guests in February of 2019. We're really enjoying meeting people!  We're both members of the Preservation Resource Center and committed to historic renovations.  We've been able to restore and reuse many original parts of this home that goes back over 100 years (still researching the history). For renovation aspects we've settled in the early 1900s, period-wise, but decided that modern kitchens and baths are a must-have.  We hope you will love it as much as we do!

Other than full-time jobs for both of us, we're typically around home most of the time.  We're interested in giving our guests as much privacy as they like, and we're not opposed to making new friends either!  Feel free to message us if you'd like to get together for a drink.  Welcome to our home. 

Cheers, 

Cody & Leo

neighborhood_overview:
Faubourg is a French term meaning 'suburb' or neighborhood. The Faubourg Tremé, or as it is more frequently referred to, Tremé, is not only America's oldest black neighborhood, but was also the site of significant economic, cultural, political, social, and legal events that have shaped the course of events in Black America for the past two centuries.

History
New Orleans' Tremé neighborhood is geographically the part of the city that lies between North Rampart and North Broad, and from Canal Street to St. Bernard Avenue. The area received its namesake from Claude Tremé, a model hat maker and real estate developer who migrated from Saugivny in Burgundy, France, and settled in New Orleans in 1783. Tremé owned only a small portion of the area that bore his name and was in possession of it for just a decade.

neighborhood_overview:
One of the most scenic and historic streets in New Orleans, Esplanade Avenue is a hidden treasure running through the heart of the city. From its beginning at the foot of the Mississippi River levee to its terminus at the entrance of City Park, Esplanade is a slow pace thoroughfare with quiet ambiance and local charm.

History
In the 19th century Esplanade was an important portage route of trade between Bayou St. John, which linked to Lake Pontchartrain, and the Mississippi River. Many 19th century mansions still line the street that once functioned as a "millionaire's row" for the Louisiana Creole section of the city, similar to that of St. Charles Avenue in Uptown New Orleans.

New Orleans Restoration Properties, owned by Marcy and Paul, is a fourth generation full service real estate development company that specializes in the restoration of historic properties.

NOLA RP’s Mission is to contribute to the Revitalization of Historic Neighborhoods by providing high quality restored properties for consumers to participate in neighborhood redevelopment through the purchasing and renting of formerly blighted properties. Lower Garden District residents have committed to preserving the neighborhood’s rich architectural history. neighborhood_overview:
Faubourg is a French term meaning 'suburb' or neighborhood. The Faubourg Tremé, or as it is more frequently referred to, Tremé, is not only America's oldest black neighborhood, but was also the site of significant economic, cultural, political, social, and legal events that have shaped the course of events in Black America for the past two centuries.

History
New Orleans' Tremé neighborhood is geographically the part of the city that lies between North Rampart and North Broad, and from Canal Street to St. Bernard Avenue. The area received its namesake from Claude Tremé, a model hat maker and real estate developer who migrated from Saugivny in Burgundy, France, and settled in New Orleans in 1783. Tremé owned only a small portion of the area that bore his name and was in possession of it for just a decade

name: Pet-Friendly Irish Channel home base
description:
COME AND SPEND MOTHER'S DAY WITH US!!!

host_about:
We both were born and raised in New Orleans. New Orleanians embrace the term “Southern Hospitality.” New Orleans is a tourist/hospitality based economy, which is rich in southern culture; from the food, the history, the architecture, and most importantly, the people. 

Chris is a Real Estate Developer and Home Builder and he loves what he does! He loves to take old historic homes and bringing them back to life. And Ashley loves to manage, decorate these homes and mostly, communicate with our guests and making their stay as enjoyable as possible. The vacation rental business gives us the opportunity to share our home with not only locals in New Orleans but people around the world. New Orleans has some of the oldest homes in the country and there is a lot of history in each house! We look forward to sharing this history with our guests. 

When we’re not working, we enjoy the outdoors, traveling the world, spending time with our Golden Retriever, Amber and family and friends. Louisiana is known as “the Sportsman’s Paradise.” Chris loves to hunt and fish as well! We both are sports junkies. Chris is a HUGE LSU fan and funny thing…Ashley is a Bama fan…so house divided here! We both love Saints football as well!

We both love to entertain and we firmly believe by doing this, it provides a great opportunity to provide the best travel experience for our guests so much that we decided to share our home with our guests..that right there is Southern Hospitality at its finest! 
We look forward to hosting you in New Orleans!

Ashley & Chris

name: Purple People Eater of Uptown!
description:
THE BEST location. Easy walking distance to fabulous restaurants, great shopping (including groceries), libraries and playgrounds for kids. You'd be less than a block from a #11 bus stop and 6 blocks from the streetcar, close to universities. If you're here during Mardi Gras, you'll be so spoiled by the location you won't want to leave.

It's an especially great apartment for families and if you need additional kids gear, we will likely be able to help provide that for your use as well.
neighborhood_overview:
A truly fantastic neighborhood! Easy walking distance to fabulous restaurants, great shopping (including Winn-Dixie, Rouse's and Whole Foods), libraries and playgrounds for kids. We're a mile from Audubon Park and mere blocks from two great playgrounds and a dog park. We're about 6 blocks from arguably the best snoballs in town (Hansen's) and have 4 restaurants in less than a block. If you expand it out to 5 blocks, there are more like 20 with such amazing variety of foods, from highbrow cuisine to pizza by the slice, from gelato to dive bars. You will never be at a loss of where to grab a bite to eat or a drink.
We're also about 6 blocks from the shopping strip on Prytania and just a few more to the Prytania theater.
Parades during Mardi Gras are less than a block away (but you'd be surprised at how NOT loud/crazy it is at our house).
We had no idea how great this spot was when we moved in--you're going to be thrilled.

name: Summerland
description: Whether you’re looking for a romantic getaway, a peaceful weekend or a great location for exploring New Orleans, my house just might be perfect for you. host_about:
I had been coming to New Orleans since 1988, and it was constantly pulling me back. As a radio professional for over 40 years, I had for 7 consecutive years produced, engineered and hosted a live one and a-half-hour show in the Boston area that I innovated, and named “I Love A Parade!”

A parade of artists from all venues, musicians of all genres, and craftspeople all from many places came into the studio to play and converse about life, their artforms, on what they were currently working, music that inspires them, and a lot of laughs. I narrated all kinds of original, improvisational, and published writing, and shared all kinds of music - with an ear to theme and segue and mostly music from New Orleans! 

Friends were often asking me, “When are you moving to New Orleans?” ~ maybe ‘cuz of what I put out there, or that the show was named “I Love A Parade!” (A new similar podcast from the house is coming soon! Maybe you can be a part of it!”)!

With all this, I woke up one snowy day, covers clutched to my chin, and looking at the ceiling, said loudly, without hesitation, “I’m movin’ to New Orleans!!”

So I cleared out the house, sold it and my cars, loaded up my son’s car, called the dog into the backseat, and with my two cats, my son and all, drove down from Somerville, MA (the NOLA of the U.S. North) to New Orleans! So glad!

Since then, I bought a house and a car, and now Christy’s Place. We named it Summerland, and now I get to meet you! Fun!

neighborhood_overview: Everyone agrees. Uptown’s got the looks in the family, bless its heart. Those handsome neighborhoods, like the St. Charles Avenue streetcar, trundle upriver, unfolding as a series of distinctive names: Oretha Castle Haley, The Garden District, Irish Channel, Riverside, the Black Pearl, Carrollton. Uptown’s homes -- gleaming white and tiered like wedding cakes or shot-gunned into long, narrow lots – are the place’s glory and sheltered by canopies of leafy green or family trees as branched and blossoming as any ancient magnolia. The air’s opulent with the scent of jasmine and a slower, grander age. Uptown, where white tablecloths still cover two-tops. The waiter knows both your name and your preferences. A gin fizz? We both love Saints football as well!

We both love to entertain and we firmly believe by doing this, it provides a great opportunity to provide the best travel experience for our guests so much that we decided to share our home with our guests..that right there is Southern Hospitality at its finest! 
We look forward to hosting you in New Orleans!

Ashley & Chris

We both were born and raised in New Orleans. New Orleanians embrace the term “Southern Hospitality.” New Orleans is a tourist/hospitality based economy, which is rich in southern culture; from the food, the history, the architecture, and most importantly, the people.

Ashley & Chris

description: This clean and bright 3 bedroom, 2 bath home is located in the prettiest part of Treme, the second oldest neighborhood in New Orleans. neighborhood_overview: New Orleans Treme neighborhood, located next to the French Quarter, is one of the most historic neighborhoods you will find in America.  It is  the birthplace of Jazz, boasting history and personality. Home to many landmarks including Armstrong Park, Congo Square, St Louis Cemetary No 1 ( where the tomb of the VooDoo Queen Marie Laveau is located) St Louis Cemetery No 2, Mahalia Jackson Theater and the Saenger Theater.  James Beard award winning restaurants Dooky Chase and Willie Mae's are located in the Treme, as well as many  other great food establishments, serving creole, soul, and many other southern specialties. Of course, there are countless locations offering cocktails, coffee or both! This home is in close proximity to historic St. Augustine Church (1841), which provides periodic church bell melodies. neighborhood_overview: The Faubourg Marigny, commonly just Marigny, is a hip neighborhood just "below" (down river from) the French Quarter. Best known for the great live music district on Frenchmen Street, the Marigny also offers neighborhood cafes & businesses, historic architecture, and more. It has the air of what the French Quarter was in it's golden days. It has a few small hotels, and many bed-and-breakfasts, as well as a number of good restaurants, coffee shops, and music venues. Architecturally, the Marigny is known for its many styles of Creole cottages, most of which date to the 19th century. Its "heart" is Washington Square Park (bounded by Frenchmen Street, Royal Street, Dauphine Street, and Elysian Fields Avenue). Frenchmen Street is the main nightlife district, with half a dozen live music clubs and just as many restaurants in four short blocks. At Mardi Gras, the Marigny is one of the city's hidden hot spots. Very popular with locals, who enjoy partying in the streets without the busy atmosph

neighborhood_overview:
The home is nestled in a safe location on Josephine Street. The Lower Garden District offers incredible shopping and immaculate cuisine.

The Lower Garden District is famous for its parks, restaurants, and history!

The area was originally developed between 1832 and 1900 and is considered one of the best-preserved collections of historic mansions in the Southern United States. The 19th-century origins of the Garden District illustrate wealthy newcomers building opulent structures based upon the prosperity of New Orleans in that era.

This whole area was once a number of plantations, including the Livaudais Plantation. It was sold off in parcels to mainly wealthy Americans who did not want to live in the French Quarter with the Creoles. It became a part of the city of Lafayette in 1833, and was annexed by New Orleans in 1852. The district was laid out by New Orleans architect, planner, and surveyor Barthelemy Lafon.

It is not in the French Quarter. Or in a retirement community.It is for travelers looking to experience the liveliness and culture of the real New Orleans.

host_about:
Thanks for checking out my profile! I am a Scottish native with a masters degree in mechanical engineering. I have lived in and around the New Orleans area for a number of years, and have an outsiders perspective combined with a locals knowledge - the perfect mix!

New Orleans is my much loved adopted home, and I reside in the best area of it with my son. I have a wide range of interests, from climbing and football to astronomy and eco-housing. I believe in a world where strangers can be family for a day and enjoy using airbnb and other similar sites. I have worked with a local international youth hostel in the area and so know a good amount about the fun things to do and see around New Orleans - and also I have plenty of 'off-the-beaten-path' ideas to share with travelers.

I love to travel, my favourite transportation style is cycling and I just did a very nice bike ride through Germany and Czech Republic. It makes me happy listening to others crazy travel plans.

That's a little bit about me, feel free to ask me anything else you would like to know.

Best known for the great live music district on Frenchmen Street, the Marigny also offers neighborhood cafes & businesses, historic architecture, and more. It has the air of what the French Quarter was in it's golden days. It has a few small hotels, and many bed-and-breakfasts, as well as a number of good restaurants, coffee shops, and music venues. Architecturally, the Marigny is known for its many styles of Creole cottages, most of which date to the 19th century. Its "heart" is Washington Square Park (bounded by Frenchmen Street, Royal Street, Dauphine Street, and Elysian Fields Avenue). Frenchmen Street is the main nightlife district, with half a dozen live music clubs and just as many restaurants in four short blocks. neighborhood_overview:
Faubourg Marigny was actually the 1st subdivision in New Orleans that developed from a factory area to the culturally rich neighborhood filled with Creole cottages that it is today.

The City of New Orleans started with just the area now known as the “Vieux Carre,” or the “French Quarter.” New Orleans grew north from Rampart Street into what is now Faubourg Treme, eventually linking up to Bayou St. John, in what is now “Mid City.” As the city continued to grow, plantation owners began breaking up their tracts of land into smaller lots to sell to newcomers. The first plantation owner to do this, Bernard Marigny de Mandeville, owned the land just downriver from Esplanade Avenue.

As more and more French people came to the area, the demand for residential property became greater. By 1805, exiles from both France and Haiti flocked to the city in the wake of revolutions. Forty years of Spanish control of Louisiana attracted a number of people from Spain and her colonies

We also enjoy describing the local creole/cajun cuisine, music, architecture culture and charm of Nola, the city we fell in love at first sight. Kindly wine, dine & recline in our tavern & guesthouse.

Architecturally, the Marigny is known for its many styles of Creole cottages, most of which date to the 19th century. Its "heart" is Washington Square Park (bounded by Frenchmen Street, Royal Street, Dauphine Street, and Elysian Fields Avenue). Frenchmen Street is the main nightlife district, with half a dozen live music clubs and just as many restaurants in four short blocks. Originally from New Orleans, moved to Texas after Katrina. Been in Denison since 2015 when I found and bought this beautiful 25-acre property. But as all things change, in getting ready to be where I want to be we bought 
a 1940s Arts and Craft Raised Cottage in the High Demand

I know it is a great neighborhood because we bought this house two doors down from my son and his wife’s house.  After a year and a half renovation which included raising the original house and constructing a new first floor (owner’s quarters) and designing the entire second floor as a separate AirBnB facility it is ready for you.  The original 1500 square foot house, consisting of three bedrooms, two bathrooms, full kitchen, laundry room and living room also include massive front and rear balconies from which you can see the city skyline.  Check out the listing in New Orleans under the heading “CRESCENT CITY VIEW”. 
The New Orleans property is available NOW and is licensed with the City of New Orleans. 
Update - In March 2022 we purchased a 4 bedroom home in Gulf Shores, AL where our back yard is on the Intercostal Waterway on  quiet street, yet in the middle of all the activities Gulf Shores has to offer. Just 3 miles from the beach by car and even shorter distance by our boat to Perdido Pass and the Gulf of Mexico. 
You will find that we strive for quality in our homes, the facility and the hospitality you will experience in New Orleans. Hope to see you soon.

neighborhood_overview:
Bywater is one of the best neighborhoods in New Orleans. It has a rich history and is an eclectic mix of fantastic restaurants, bakeries, bars, art studios and more. It has long been home to some of New Orleans' famous artists and musicians. The neighborhood is very walkable and the home is two block from Crescent Park and the Mississippi.

There are tons of local cafes, restaurants and bars that are unique to New Orleans (many of which are dog friendly). You can’t leave New Orleans without exploring the Bywater/Marigny neighborhoods and seeing how locals live and eat.
There is an abandoned navy base across the way that many people explore since it’s a little piece of history.

City Blue Bikes right around the corner from you!

Near parade route!

neighborhood_overview:
Bywater is a neighborhood of the city of New Orleans. A subdistrict of the Bywater District Area, its boundaries as defined by the City Planning Commission are: Florida Avenue to the north, the Industrial Canal to the east, the Mississippi River to the south, and the railroad tracks along Homer Plessy Way (formerly Press Street) to the west. Bywater is part of the Ninth Ward of New Orleans; but it is located along the natural levee of the Mississippi River, sparing the area from significant flooding. It includes part or all of Bywater Historic District, which is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.[1]

host_about:
We both were born and raised in New Orleans. New Orleanians embrace the term “Southern Hospitality.” New Orleans is a tourist/hospitality based economy, which is rich in southern culture; from the food, the history, the architecture, and most importantly, the people. 

Chris is a Real Estate Developer and Home Builder and he loves what he does! He loves to take old historic homes and bringing them back to life. And Ashley loves to manage, decorate these homes and mostly, communicate with our guests and making their stay as enjoyable as possible. The vacation rental business gives us the opportunity to share our home with not only locals in New Orleans but people around the world. New Orleans has some of the oldest homes in the country and there is a lot of history in each house! We look forward to sharing this history with our guests. 

When we’re not working, we enjoy the outdoors, traveling the world, spending time with our Golden Retriever, Amber and family and friends. Louisiana is known as “the Sportsman’s Paradise.” Chris loves to hunt and fish as well! We both are sports junkies. Chris is a HUGE LSU fan and funny thing…Ashley is a Bama fan…so house divided here! We both love Saints football as well!

We both love to entertain and we firmly believe by doing this, it provides a great opportunity to provide the best travel experience for our guests so much that we decided to share our home with our guests..that right there is Southern Hospitality at its finest! 
We look forward to hosting you in New Orleans!

Ashley & Chris

Ashley & Chris

Located Uptown near the river bend, the culturally diverse Leonidas neighborhood has history dating all the way back to the 1700s. Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville, a French colonizer and the founder of the city of New Orleans, began a plantation in the area circa 1719.[6] The land went on to remain a plantation for different types of agriculture well into the 1800s. The area was then bought by the New Orleans Canal and Banking Company and was divided into sections. In 1835, the first house was built and soon emerged a new neighborhood of the city of New Orleans.[6] The Leonidas neighborhood was a part of a bigger whole called the town of Carrollton. In the 1850s, Dublin was the main street of the town. The current-day commerce corridor is Oak Street.

It has the air of what the French Quarter was in it's golden days. It has a few small hotels, and many bed-and-breakfasts, as well as a number of good restaurants, coffee shops, and music venues. Architecturally, the Marigny is known for its many styles of Creole cottages, most of which date to the 19th century. Its "heart" is Washington Square Park (bounded by Frenchmen Street, Royal Street, Dauphine Street, and Elysian Fields Avenue). Frenchmen Street is the main nightlife district, with half a dozen live music clubs and just as many restaurants in four short blocks. host_about:
Local New Orleanian, born in Europe raised in New Orleans. 

There's no place like home...especially when home is New Orleans. The city is one of those unicorn travel destinations — the kind that’s both totally bucket-list-worthy yet also a place you'll want to return to time and time again.

New Orleans is truly amazing - it's small enough to be able to experience it all - good food, arts, nightlife, culture, music, local festivals throughout the year and so much more.

"There are many places I like, but I like New Orleans better." - Bob Dylan

“America has only three cities: New York, San Francisco, and New Orleans. Everywhere else is Cleveland.” - Tennessee Williams

"Oh, the places you'll go!" - Dr. Seuss

"In America, there might be better gastronomic destinations than New Orleans, but there is no place more uniquely wonderful. ... With the best restaurants in New York, you'll find something similar to it in Paris or Copenhagen or Chicago. But there is no place like New Orleans. So it's a must-see city because there's no explaining it, no describing it. You can't compare it to anything. So, far and away, New Orleans." - Anthony Bourdain

"To me, New Orleans has always been a town that lived outside of the laws of regular society, and I believe New Orleans has always been that way. It doesn’t really participate in America. It has its own rules, its own cultures, its own conditions, and it really doesn’t care what you think." - John Waters 

"...Go because it's crazy, borderline dysfunctional, permissive, shabby, alcoholic and crazy --- and because it looks like nowhere else." - Anthony Bourdain

neighborhood_overview:
Fontainebleau-Marleyville is one of New Orleans’ most quiet, safe, and convenient neighborhoods. It is characterized by large canopy trees, quiet streets, a convenient location, and an old-fashioned neighborhood atmosphere.

Historically, Fontainebleau-Marleyville is one of New Orleans’ newer neighborhoods, with its roots stretching only to the turn of the 20th century. name: Central Charm | 1 mile to Superdome & Parades |
description:
This spacious & charming home is located in a true NOLA neighborhood & is indeed central to everything! It is 1 mile away from both the Garden & Central Business Districts (downtown), 1 mile from super dome, 1.6 miles from Bourbon, & 2-3 miles from the rest of the infamous French Quarter.

2 bedrooms (4 beds), 2 bathrooms, a fully stocked kitchen with an island & a dining table, & an open concept floor plan. Recently renovated. Each room has its own AC/heat unit adjustable by remote control.
neighborhood_overview: Central City is a true NOLA neighborhood. It is indeed central to everything- the Central Business District (downtown), Garden District and the rest of Uptown. It is known for the Mardi Gras Day parades and Second Lines (you may see a second line roll by on a Sunday afternoon). It is within a historical district and is in the process of gentrification and rebuilding. Most of the houses were built in the early 1900's and display the traditional bright colors with French style architecture. You'll see a true New Orleans neighborhood with a variety of house styles- shotgun singles, shotgun doubles, cottages, victorian, brick rebuilds, new construction and blighted houses around the corner as well- and a variety of people, mostly native/locals, kids that like to practice their brass instruments after school, and some that have moved here from other places. This is a true, historical NOLA neighborhood that is as mixed as they come- just like the GUMBO that is New Orleans!
host_about: Originally born in Nola and raised in ATL- but a Saints fan till the end! I've lived in Nola the last 10 years. I love exploring to find the best food, fun, music, & shopping. The culture is engrained & I look forward to sharing it with you!

name: Balcony & City Views: 2BR Retreat near Superdome
description:
Welcome to your New Orleans getaway.
- Charming 2BR apartment with private entrance, high-speed WiFi, HDTVs with Netflix, and a fully equipped kitchen.
- Family-friendly perks include a Pack 'n Play, central A/C and high chair.
- Unwind on the private balcony with neighborhood views.

- Convenient base for your NOLA adventure.
neighborhood_overview:
Steps to Endymion and Zulu Parades during Mardi Gras!

North of the noise and saturated color of the Quarter is a New Orleans neighborhood that’s perfected the art of living. “Welcome to Mid-City,” read the signs on the neutral ground. And that’s truth in advertising. It’s the kind of place where your auto mechanic invites you to a crawfish boil and a total stranger may buy you a drink at an Irish pub or a cannoli at an Italian bakery. Take the red streetcar line up Canal to the Cemeteries (Mid-City’s dead neighbors are as interesting as the live ones) or bike the new 2.6-mile-long Lafitte Greenway that stretches from Basin Street to Carrollton Avenue and, conveniently, past a po’ boy shop or two – or 17 – with a sno-ball shop and a micro-brewery thrown in for good measure. Buttermilk biscuits. Live music. A bowl of Vietnamese pho. Who wouldn’t want to visit? Eat. Drink. Get up here.
If you have any questions about the neighborhood, please send us a message!

Offering a unique blend of comfort and local charm, our properties are nestled in the city's most vibrant neighborhoods.

Experience authentic Creole cuisine, jazz, and the magic of The Big Easy. Explore Bourbon Street's nightlife, relax by the Mississippi, and immerse yourself in local festivals.

neighborhood_overview:
Carrollton is the section of New Orleans that is at the far end of Uptown from the French Quarter, between the Audubon & University District of New Orleans and Jefferson Parish. It is often considered part of Uptown, but it has its own history and traditions (including being a separate city in the 19th century), so it will be treated on its own here. The high ground of the "Carrollton Spur" was fortunately above the great flood which devastated much of the New Orleans area after Hurricane Katrina in 2005, leaving this charming neighborhood intact.


Oak Street has restaurants, shops, cafes, bars, and live music venues.
It is at the far end of the St. Charles Streetcar line (the green cars) whose other end is on Canal Street in the Central Business District. Carrollton is near Tulane and Loyola Universities and many students and professors live here and patronize the local businesses. neighborhood_overview:
Steps to Endymion and Zulu Parades during Mardi Gras!

North of the noise and saturated color of the Quarter is a New Orleans neighborhood that’s perfected the art of living. “Welcome to Mid-City,” read the signs on the neutral ground. And that’s truth in advertising. It’s the kind of place where your auto mechanic invites you to a crawfish boil and a total stranger may buy you a drink at an Irish pub or a cannoli at an Italian bakery. Take the red streetcar line up Canal to the Cemeteries (Mid-City’s dead neighbors are as interesting as the live ones) or bike the new 2.6-mile-long Lafitte Greenway that stretches from Basin Street to Carrollton Avenue and, conveniently, past a po’ boy shop or two – or 17 – with a sno-ball shop and a micro-brewery thrown in for good measure. Buttermilk biscuits. Live music. A bowl of Vietnamese pho. Who wouldn’t want to visit? Eat. Drink. Get up here.
If you have any questions about the neighborhood, please send us a message!

description:
Your family will be close to everything when you stay at this centrally-located uptown apartment just steps from both Tulane and Loyola.

An easy walk to Audubon Park, Audubon Zoo, St. Charles Streetcar, Freret Street dining and Riverfront park (the Fly). You'll love just strolling around the neighborhood admiring the people and architecture that make New Orleans great.
neighborhood_overview: Everyone agrees. Uptown’s got the looks in the family, bless its heart. Those handsome neighborhoods, like the St. Charles Avenue streetcar, trundle upriver, unfolding as a series of distinctive names: Oretha Castle Haley, The Garden District, Irish Channel, Riverside, the Black Pearl, Carrollton. Uptown’s homes -- gleaming white and tiered like wedding cakes or shot-gunned into long, narrow lots – are the place’s glory and sheltered by canopies of leafy green or family trees as branched and blossoming as any ancient magnolia. The air’s opulent with the scent of jasmine and a slower, grander age. Uptown, where white tablecloths still cover two-tops. The waiter knows both your name and your preferences. A gin fizz? The crabmeat salad? Satsuma orange ice cream? They’re all on offer, as are the dazzling array of goods. The smart shops on Oak and Maple, Freret and Magazine, rival anything anywhere else. But this is Uptown, sugar. Once you’re here, there’s no reason – not ever – to leave.<b
host_about: I Live in New Orleans with my wife and two lovely children.  We love all the food and entertainment that New Orleans offers.  We want everyone to come to NOLA and leave with amazing memories.

Start your morning with a cup of coffee and breakfast at the Treme Coffee House or Fatma’s Cozy Corner, both just a half-a-block away.

neighborhood_overview:
Steps to Endymion and Zulu Parades during Mardi Gras!

North of the noise and saturated color of the Quarter is a New Orleans neighborhood that’s perfected the art of living. “Welcome to Mid-City,” read the signs on the neutral ground. And that’s truth in advertising. It’s the kind of place where your auto mechanic invites you to a crawfish boil and a total stranger may buy you a drink at an Irish pub or a cannoli at an Italian bakery. Take the red streetcar line up Canal to the Cemeteries (Mid-City’s dead neighbors are as interesting as the live ones) or bike the new 2.6-mile-long Lafitte Greenway that stretches from Basin Street to Carrollton Avenue and, conveniently, past a po’ boy shop or two – or 17 – with a sno-ball shop and a micro-brewery thrown in for good measure. Buttermilk biscuits. Live music. A bowl of Vietnamese pho. Who wouldn’t want to visit? Eat. Drink. Get up here.
If you have any questions about the neighborhood, please send us a message!

The home is nestled in a safe location on Josephine Street. The Lower Garden District offers incredible shopping and immaculate cuisine.

The Lower Garden District is famous for its parks, restaurants, and history!

The area was originally developed between 1832 and 1900 and is considered one of the best-preserved collections of historic mansions in the Southern United States. The 19th-century origins of the Garden District illustrate wealthy newcomers building opulent structures based upon the prosperity of New Orleans in that era.

This whole area was once a number of plantations, including the Livaudais Plantation. It was sold off in parcels to mainly wealthy Americans who did not want to live in the French Quarter with the Creoles. It became a part of the city of Lafayette in 1833, and was annexed by New Orleans in 1852. The district was laid out by New Orleans architect, planner, and surveyor Barthelemy Lafon.

neighborhood_overview:
Once the most prestigious Creole neighborhoods in the city, the Esplanade Ridge Historic District boasts one of the largest and most impressive concentrations of historic buildings in the nation.

Esplanade Avenue, with its great width, is the spine of this District and contains its largest houses. In 1807, an act of Congress gave the City of New Orleans title to a strip of land that would become Esplanade Avenue, located on a ridge between the Mississippi River and Bayou St. John. This ridge was the site of an ancient Native American portage.

The Esplanade Ridge Historic District illustrates the development along this ridge from Claiborne Avenue to Bayou St. John.

This neighborhood is right next to the French Quarter, and close to everything fun.

Located on the northern border of the French Quarter above Rampart Street, Tremé is a uniquely historic neighborhood--one of the oldest neighborhoods in New Orleans. Early in the city's history, it was the main neighborhood of free people of color, and remains an important center of the city's Creole culture, especially the modern brass band tradition.
The modern Tremé neighborhood began as the Morand Plantation and two forts—St. Ferdinand and St. John. Near the end of the 18th century, Claude Tremé purchased the land from the original plantation owner. Within a few decades, the Carondelet Canal was built from the French Quarter to Bayou St. John, splitting the land. Developers began building subdivisions throughout the area to house a diverse population.

Part of the larger Mid City area in New Orleans, the Fairgrounds neighborhood takes its name from the Fair Grounds Race Course that sits in the middle of it.

Mostly residential, the predominant architectural types are raised cottages, Arts & Crafts cottages, townhouse style, and shotguns. The Fairgrounds neighborhood is filled with renovated homes and even a smattering of new construction.

You’ll find residents walking and biking all over, with a WalkScore of 69 (mostly on the south and southeast sides of the track) and a BikeScore of 83. It’s so easy to grab breakfast at Toast, cocktails at Brooks Seahorse Saloon, a po-boy at Liuzza’s by the Track, coffee at CC’s, or visit St. Louis Cemetery #3. The neighborhood is bordered by Bayou St. John, so you’ll be near City Park, the New Orleans Museum of Art and the outdoor activities that happen along the bayou.

neighborhood_overview:
Located between Uptown and Downtown along the Mississippi River, the Irish Channel is a historic neighborhood full of colorful homes, local charm, and a whole lot of character. It’s a great spot to experience the real New Orleans—relaxed, walkable, and full of things to discover.

You’re just five blocks from Magazine Street and less than a mile from St. Charles Avenue—two of the city’s most iconic streets. The address has a Walk Score of 85 (Very Walkable), so getting around on foot is easy and enjoyable.

Grab coffee around the corner, explore local shops and restaurants, or hop on the streetcar for a scenic ride to Audubon Park, the universities, or the French Quarter. Most places in the New Orleans metro are less than a 30-minute drive, making this a super convenient home base—whether you’re here for work, play, or a bit of both.

neighborhood_overview:
The St. Roch neighborhood of New Orleans has many landmarks that can be considered to hold significant historical value. One of the older landmarks of St. Roch is the market in the neighborhood known simply as the St. Roch Market. It was built in 1875 as an open-air market on St. Claude Avenue.

The St. Roch chapel is located in the cemetery. It is filled with prosthetics, crutches, and other ex-votos of those who visit the chapel to ask St. Roch for healing. name: Holy Cross Garden Suite w lap pool and jacuzzi
description: Holy Cross retreat with a salt water lap pool (clothing optional), jacuzzi, garden, and just a block and a half from the Mississippi River levee park with best sunset views of New Orleans. Sit on the wrap around porch in a rocking chair and look out over the pool. Or enjoy the a/c or heat and high speed wifi (500Mbps) to get your work done. Relax in an Eames lounge chair and catch up on your reading. Take a jog along the river or do laps to stay in shape. The perfect getaway or remote work spot.
neighborhood_overview: Holy Cross Neighborhood is a very quiet residential neighborhood just across the canal from Bywater and about 2 miles downriver from the French Quarter. The neighborhood is named after the old Holy Cross School, which was built in 1849 and is located just across the street from our property. (See photos). The school was abandoned after Hurricane Katrina, but is now under restoration and being turned into apartments. The Levee Park is the crowning jewel of the neighborhood as it has the best sunset views in the entire city. There are benches scattered along the river and there is even a set of swings. Another famous landmark in the neighborhood is the Doullut Steamboat house (see photo). The levee park is the place to be when the sun begins to fall: revealers from around the city come to picnic at sunset; and even in the summer, there is usually a cool breeze that makes watching the sunset on the levee a year round activity.
host_about:
Sasha grew up in the New York suburbs and when he first came to New Orleans as an 18 year old, it was love at first sight. He moved here the following year, in 1999 and has been here ever since. Sasha has lived mostly in the downtown neighborhoods of the French Quarter, Marigny, Bywater, and Lower 9th Ward. He worked in the City's Restaurant and Music scene, gay bar circuit, and studied Louisiana history at Tulane University; so, he can answer any questions you might have about the city. 

Franco, Sasha's partner, is from Mexico City and has lived in New Orleans since 2016. He is a makeup artist and has also worked a variety of other jobs in and around the city. He is big fan of all kinds of music and loves hanging out in the French Quarter.

neighborhood_overview:
As one of the oldest neighborhoods in New Orleans, the Bayou St. John area boasts a more secluded and peaceful atmosphere of the city. Bayou St. John is known for its haven of tree-lined streets and avenues, gardens, and galleries. It is often referred to as one of the most historic neighborhoods in New Orleans and frequented for its beautiful, natural environment.

If you’re looking to relax or take a contemplative stroll, this largely residential neighborhood is a great way to spend the day by the gentle waters of the bayou. But just as it’s gentle waters flow through the neighborhood so does the history of the city.

History

Also called the Faubourg St. John neighborhood, the neighborhood is bounded by Bayou Road/Gentilly Boulevard and Belfort Avenue to the north, Orleans Avenue to the South, as well as North Broad Street to the East. The Bayou St. John creates its Western boundaries.

neighborhood_overview:
From a neighborhood of working class immigrants to one of the hottest neighborhoods in the city, the Irish Channel has a long and storied history.

The Irish Channel was originally home to many of the Irish workers who came here in the 1830s to build the New Basin Canal, a waterway built to connect Lake Pontchartrain with businesses and industry in the developing New Orleans.

This neighborhood is known for its small cottages and shotgun homes located on narrow lots, traditionally inhabited by blue-collar workers who could afford their modest prices. House here are smaller than in the Garden District or in other parts of Uptown, but what they lack in square footage, they make up for in fine decoration charm. Their close proximity creates a feeling of community and coziness. Here you can still ask a neighbor for a cup of sugar or gossip over a backyard fence.
